scope: Q2 technology evaluation; Q3 portfolio design is being developed by the user. Earth first; space comparison boundary only.

records.name: Solar photovoltaics
records.service: Converts sunlight directly to electricity. Silicon and cadmium-telluride are established products.
records.evidence: Large factories and operating fleets. LONGi reports 86.58 GW of modules shipped in 2025; First Solar reports 17.5 GW sold. These are manufacturer DC module figures, not measured electricity or AC plant capacity.
records.companies: LONGi: public, founder-controlled in its June 2026 filing; sales and debt finance factories. First Solar: public shareholders; sales, corporate capital and US manufacturing credits. Plant developers raise separate project capital.
records.cost: US$44/MWh: global average estimate for projects commissioned in 2025. US$40–98/MWh: modeled US new builds in 2026. Generation only; not all-hours supply.
records.demand_and_timing: IEA 2050 scenarios: 20,374–35,509 TWh/year, or 35.1–44.3% of each scenario total. Main near-term growth option, subject to connections and demand at generating hours.
records.limitations: Night, seasonal variation, midday surplus, land/roofs, transmission and financing. More panel efficiency does not remove these constraints.
records.geopolitics: China-centered supply chains make tariffs, import restrictions and local manufacturing policy economically important.
records.assessment: Very strong evidence of scalable generation. Compare delivered local projects and hourly value, not just module efficiency.

records.name: Perovskite-silicon tandem solar
records.service: Adds a second light-absorbing layer to capture more energy per unit area.
records.evidence: Oxford PV reported first commercial shipment in 2024. A laboratory cell record, factory module result and multi-year field performance are different evidence.
records.companies: Oxford PV is private; historical backers include Goldwind, Equinor and Legal & General. Exact current control was not verified. LONGi also pursues higher-efficiency solar; that does not make all its output tandem.
records.cost: No independently established commercial fleet electricity cost. Higher efficiency helps only if price, yield and lifetime preserve the gain.
records.demand_and_timing: Potentially increases solar output where land or installation cost matters. Included within the solar scenario totals; no separate verified 2050 share.
records.limitations: Outdoor degradation, moisture/heat, encapsulation, large-area manufacturing yield and warranty backing.
records.geopolitics: European R&D/manufacturing and international intellectual property compete with established Asian scale.
records.assessment: Credible solar improvement to track. Require full-module lifetime and cost evidence before claiming a system-wide breakthrough.

records.name: Onshore wind
records.service: Converts wind into electricity using land-based turbines.
records.evidence: Vestas reported 201 GW cumulatively installed by end-2025, across onshore and offshore models. Historical installations are not all necessarily still operating.
records.companies: Vestas: listed, broadly held; sales, services and corporate finance. Other major suppliers include Chinese and European manufacturers; the detailed ledger does not claim an exhaustive supplier ranking.
records.cost: US$33/MWh global commissioned-project average in 2025; US$37–99/MWh modeled US new builds in 2026.
records.demand_and_timing: IEA all-wind scenarios: 10,991–23,250 TWh/year in 2050, 18.9–29.0% of respective totals. Do not allocate the full total separately to onshore and offshore wind.
records.limitations: Wind variation, land access, permitting, transmission, turbine reliability and maintenance.
records.geopolitics: Local-content rules, trade restrictions and manufacturing location change project bids and eligibility.
records.assessment: A strong low-cost generation benchmark. Evaluate regional wind resource and production timing alongside buildability.

records.name: Fixed-bottom offshore wind
records.service: Wind turbines anchored to the seabed; an ocean-sited wind technology, distinct from wave and tidal energy.
records.evidence: Commercial offshore turbines and fleets exist; new projects still carry installation and repair risk.
records.companies: Vestas is a detailed supplier example. Developers, utilities and infrastructure investors finance individual farms separately from turbine manufacturers.
records.cost: US$78/MWh global 2025 commissioned-project average; US$105–167/MWh modeled US 2026 projects. Geographic and financial differences explain part of the gap.
records.demand_and_timing: Part of the all-wind 2050 totals. Can serve large coastal demand, with build rates limited by ports, vessels, cables and connections.
records.limitations: Marine construction, access in poor weather, seabed conditions, cable failures and financing.
records.geopolitics: Seabed leasing, national procurement and industrial policy strongly affect whether projects proceed.
records.assessment: Established generation with more demanding construction economics than onshore wind. Use local bids; do not transfer its cost to floating wind.

records.name: Floating offshore wind
records.service: Places wind turbines on floating foundations moored in deep water.
records.evidence: Hywind Tampen operates with 11 turbines, 94.6 MW combined turbine rating. Operator notes export infrastructure was not upgraded with the turbines.
records.companies: Equinor: 67% Norwegian state-owned listed company; project partners and historical Enova support. State ownership, project subsidy and project ownership are distinct.
records.cost: No standardized repeat-project cost verified in this review. Fixed-bottom/global offshore averages are comparators, not floating-wind quotations.
records.demand_and_timing: Potential access to deep-water wind near coastal loads. Still a small operating base relative to established wind; no separate forecast assigned.
records.limitations: Floating foundations, moorings, dynamic cables, ports, towing/repair and financial risk.
records.geopolitics: Countries with deep coastlines and offshore industrial capability may support early projects; seabed and environmental permissions remain local.
records.assessment: Technically demonstrated at array scale. Repeated construction and maintenance costs are the main commercial test.

records.name: Hydropower and pumped storage
records.service: Natural river inflow supplies hydro generation. Pumped storage moves previously generated electricity through a water cycle and consumes net energy.
records.evidence: Large global operating fleets; reservoirs can shift output, subject to water availability and operating rules.
records.companies: Examples include utility/public operators such as EDF and K-water. Ownership and funding are typically project-specific public or utility capital plus debt.
records.cost: Conventional hydro: US$62/MWh global 2025 commissioned-project average. This is not a cost for every dam or pumped-storage discharge.
records.demand_and_timing: IEA hydro generation: 6,383–7,398 TWh/year in 2050, 11.0–9.2% of respective scenarios. Do not add pumped-storage output as new primary energy.
records.limitations: Geography, drought, competing water uses, ecosystems, displacement and civil works.
records.geopolitics: Transboundary river agreements and public investment shape access and operation.
records.assessment: Important established benchmark; expansion is site-constrained. Evaluate natural inflow and storage services separately.

records.name: Large nuclear fission
records.service: Splits atomic nuclei to provide heat, usually producing electricity through steam turbines.
records.evidence: Long operating record. KHNP/KEPCO’s four Barakah units entered service in 2021–24. New construction performance varies strongly across countries and projects.
records.companies: Westinghouse: Brookfield 51%, Cameco 49%. EDF: French state. KHNP: KEPCO subsidiary. Utilities/governments finance plants; reactor suppliers are not automatically plant owners.
records.cost: US$175–255/MWh modeled new US nuclear based on Vogtle. IEA repeat-build 2024 assumptions: China 70, India 75, US 110, EU 165 US$/MWh. Existing plant operating costs are a separate category.
records.demand_and_timing: IEA total fission, including SMRs: 5,531–6,853 TWh/year in 2050, 9.5–8.5%. New builds and retaining existing plants both affect supply.
records.limitations: Upfront capital, long construction, outages, workforce/components, fuel, cooling and waste provisions.
records.geopolitics: Government finance, export agreements and fuel suppliers shape costs and schedules; national industry matters as much as reactor design.
records.assessment: Proven large-scale generation. Evaluate the actual builder, country, finance and completed cost before comparing economics.

records.name: Small light-water reactors
records.service: Smaller reactors using familiar water-cooled technology, with a proposed path to repeated manufacture.
records.evidence: GE Vernova Hitachi’s 300 MW BWRX-300 at Darlington is under construction. Regulatory approval to construct is not permission to operate or proof of fleet cost.
records.companies: US technology venture: GE Vernova 60%, Hitachi 40%. OPG owns Darlington and finances the project; technology supplier and plant owner differ.
records.cost: OPG first-unit budget C$7.7bn includes shared infrastructure, interest, contingency and escalation. Equivalent C$25,700/kW is not an overnight or repeated-unit price.
records.demand_and_timing: IEA broad SMR cases: 40–190 GW in 2050; at our assumed 85% output, 298–1,415 TWh/year. These are subsets of fission, not extra output to add.
records.limitations: First-build cost, licensing, manufacturing orders and economies of repetition. Smaller size alone does not guarantee cheap electricity.
records.geopolitics: Public procurement can establish first orders; supply-chain localization and licensing differ by market.
records.assessment: Concrete construction evidence makes this a serious option. The key economic test is the cost of successive completed units.

records.name: Advanced fission: sodium and high-temperature designs
records.service: Uses different coolants, fuels or heat delivery. TerraPower Natrium and X-energy Xe-100 are different designs, not interchangeable products.
records.evidence: TerraPower received NRC construction authorization in March 2026 and announced plant construction in April. No operating commercial Xe-100 fleet verified here.
records.companies: TerraPower: private, Gates-founded, US$650m 2025 equity round. X-energy: public since April 2026, about US$1.1bn net IPO proceeds; Amazon earlier investor/customer. Exact current private control unknown.
records.cost: No completed commercial price for these designs. Do not turn funding rounds or proposed contract prices into verified production costs.
records.demand_and_timing: Natrium’s 345 MW reactor plus storage can vary delivery; temporary storage output is not extra reactor energy. Future output is inside fission scenarios.
records.limitations: HALEU and fuel fabrication for relevant designs, materials, first construction, maintenance and full plant licensing.
records.geopolitics: US enrichment investment and industrial-policy support address supply risk; fuel availability remains design-specific.
records.assessment: Potentially useful electricity and industrial heat, but cost and repeatability remain open. Track construction and fuel deliveries rather than announced pipeline alone.

records.name: Fusion
records.service: Combines light nuclei; different companies pursue magnetic confinement, pulsed systems and other designs.
records.status: No verified commercial net-electric plant in this review
records.evidence: CFS SPARC and Helion’s machines address important technical steps. Plasma/target gain is not the electricity balance of an entire power station.
records.companies: CFS: private, reports US$4bn cumulative funding after July 2026 round; Google and Eni are investors/buyers. Helion: private, US$500m Series G close reported September 2026, Thrive-led.
records.cost: No verified commercial electricity price. Target prices lack an operating fleet basis.
records.demand_and_timing: CFS targets ~400 MW ARC early next decade; Helion targets ≥50 MW Orion from 2028. To supply 1% of 80,000 TWh/year at assumed 85% output requires ~107 GW, or ~269 plants of 400 MW.
records.limitations: Net electricity, repetition/duty cycle, materials life, maintainability and fuel cycle; tritium requirements differ by design.
records.geopolitics: National R&D, specialized components, fuel and strategic power buyers can support development; they cannot establish performance.
records.assessment: Potentially important later; present supply contribution cannot be inferred from fundraising or first-plant targets. Require sustained net electricity and credible repeat-plant cost.

records.name: Conventional and enhanced geothermal
records.service: Uses underground heat. Conventional plants exploit suitable reservoirs; enhanced systems create or improve flow pathways.
records.status: Conventional commercial; enhanced early commercial output
records.evidence: Fervo reports first Cape Station unit operating at 33 MW net in October 2026. The full announced development was not all operating.
records.companies: Fervo is public after May 2026 IPO; reports US$2.2bn gross IPO proceeds and US$421m project debt for first phase. Equity and debt are separate financing categories.
records.cost: Conventional geothermal global 2025 average US$89/MWh. Do not label this a measured Fervo/EGS cost. IEA’s ~US$50/MWh by 2035 is a conditional improvement case.
records.demand_and_timing: IEA all-geothermal 2050 output 452–825 TWh. Separate next-generation study reaches nearly 6,000 TWh under strong cost/technology assumptions; these cases cannot be added together.
records.limitations: Well cost, sustained flow/temperature, pumping, induced seismicity, water and drilling supply.
records.geopolitics: Oilfield expertise can transfer; local subsurface/water permitting and industrial-policy support affect pace.
records.assessment: Among the strongest emerging dependable-power candidates in this comparison because early net output exists. Long reservoir performance and repeat-build cost still need proof.

records.name: Closed-loop geothermal
records.service: Circulates fluid in sealed underground wells, extracting heat without requiring a naturally permeable reservoir.
records.evidence: Eavor reported first Geretsried power in December 2025; a March 2026 research visit confirmed the first loop operating and economic assessment ongoing.
records.companies: Eavor: private; Canada Growth Fund, energy companies and other investors. June 2025 CGF commitment up to ~C$138m included a milestone-dependent portion.
records.cost: No verified commercial fleet cost. The amount of useful heat versus electricity changes the business case.
records.demand_and_timing: Potentially broadens eligible geothermal sites. No separate verified global contribution; stays inside geothermal totals.
records.limitations: Drilling cost/length, thermal transfer, long-term heat decline and site temperature.
records.geopolitics: Canadian capital, European support and district-heat infrastructure can create early markets.
records.assessment: Promising with actual first output; distinguish operating first loop from planned full-site output.

records.name: Superhot geothermal and new drilling
records.service: Seeks much hotter rock; new drilling methods may make deep heat accessible.
records.evidence: Quaise has drilling and power-project plans; no operating Quaise power plant verified here.
records.companies: Private Quaise closed US$180m Series B in August 2026; Nabors’ US$35m investment is included and gives 14% fully diluted ownership, not majority control.
records.cost: No demonstrated commercial electricity price. Hotter rock does not by itself establish a cheaper completed plant.
records.demand_and_timing: Quaise’s initial Obsidian target is 50 MW; later expansion is conditional. Do not translate theoretical heat resources into buildable 2050 output.
records.limitations: Deep drilling, well completion, extreme-temperature materials, reservoir design and sustained net output.
records.geopolitics: Drilling-contractor partnerships help industrial execution; sites still need permits and qualified suppliers.
records.assessment: High potential with substantial remaining engineering. Keep separate from Fervo’s current operating evidence.

records.name: Wave electricity exported to a grid
records.service: Captures wave motion and sends electricity ashore or to a nearby load.
records.evidence: CorPower C4 has demonstrated grid export. Its 10 MW VianaWave array is planned, with company-targeted operation in 2029/30.
records.companies: CorPower: private Swedish company, €32m 2024 equity round led by NordicNinja/SEB/EIT InnoEnergy, plus distinct EU support. Detailed control not verified.
records.cost: IRENA early-wave estimate ~US$454/MWh; conditional European learning estimate ~US$120/MWh at 2 GW cumulative deployment. The latter is not a current quote or guaranteed learning curve.
records.demand_and_timing: IEA all-marine 2050 scenarios 86–112 TWh/year. Wave has no separate verified forecast here; resource potential can exceed the scenario, but delivery must be shown.
records.limitations: Storm survival, corrosion, fatigue, marine repairs, arrays/cables, annual output and financing.
records.geopolitics: Demonstration grants and guaranteed-price procurement help early learning; permits, fisheries and ports constrain sites.
records.assessment: Credible physical generation, still weak commercial cost evidence. Compare complete array cost and metered annual output with local alternatives.

records.name: Wave-powered offshore computing
records.service: Uses wave electricity on a floating computer and exports data rather than electricity.
records.evidence: Panthalassa’s May 2026 announcement described pilots and future commercialization; independently verified commercial output/uptime was not established.
records.companies: Private public-benefit corporation; US$140m Series B led by Peter Thiel, with other financial and industrial investors. Ownership percentages undisclosed here.
records.cost: No verified complete cost per useful compute job. Avoided export cables may help, but communications, utilization and offshore maintenance add costs.
records.demand_and_timing: Addresses only computing workloads compatible with the location and communications. It does not directly meet general grid demand.
records.limitations: Variable waves, uptime, compute hardware, cooling, corrosion, storms, repairs, satellite links and data constraints.
records.geopolitics: Maritime permissions, chip supply/export rules, data rules and communications access affect the model.
records.assessment: A distinct customer proposition worth evaluating. Compare the same compute service onshore and offshore, including equipment replacement and downtime.

records.name: Tidal-stream turbines and kites
records.service: Extracts moving-water energy from tidal currents; predictable timing does not mean constant output.
records.evidence: Orbital O2 is 2 MW; MeyGen has 6 MW installed; Minesto reports extended Dragon tests. Planned arrays and contracted future MW remain separate.
records.companies: Orbital is private. MeyGen owner Ampeak is listed, with a dated 29.6% indirect Hughes holding. Minesto is public; Corespring named largest shareholder. Grants, equity, debt and supported power prices all appear.
records.cost: IRENA early-stage tidal-stream estimate ~US$358/MWh; conditional learning value ~US$140/MWh at 2 GW cumulative European deployment. No universal company bid.
records.demand_and_timing: Part of 86–112 TWh/year marine scenarios. 1% of a 60,000–80,000 TWh world would need 196–261 GW at an assumed 35% average output, far above current small arrays.
records.limitations: Usable channels, slack tides, underwater maintenance, cables, ecological effects and repeated-array finance.
records.geopolitics: UK AR7 awarded 20.9 MW of tidal contracts; these create revenue support, not immediate generation. Regional procurement continuity matters.
records.assessment: Stronger deployment evidence than an unbuilt concept; cost and location constrain scale. Evaluate site-level annual production and servicing.

records.name: Tidal range: barrages and lagoons
records.service: Uses the water-level difference across an embankment, like coastal hydropower.
records.evidence: K-water’s Sihwa plant has 254 MW installed. This is a different technology from free-stream turbines and must not inherit their cost or readiness label.
records.companies: K-water is the project operator; EDF operates another established tidal-range reference. These are infrastructure/public-utility models; full financing structures were not audited in this pass.
records.cost: No current comparable new-build cost established here. Reusing an existing embankment differs from constructing a new lagoon.
records.demand_and_timing: Potential regional output at suitable tidal ranges. No separate defensible global contribution assigned.
records.limitations: Large civil works, estuary ecology, sediment, navigation, fisheries and site availability; production varies through tidal cycles.
records.geopolitics: Public planning and coastal/environmental consent dominate the development path.
records.assessment: Technically established in selected locations; site economics and environmental acceptability decide new expansion.

records.name: Ocean thermal energy conversion
records.service: Uses warm surface water and cold deep water to run a heat engine; typically needs about 20°C temperature difference.
records.status: Small demonstrations; larger projects in development
records.evidence: EIA documents a 105 kW Hawaii demonstration operating from 2015. Global OTEC’s September 2026 Bahamas work is a feasibility study, not a generating plant.
records.companies: Global OTEC is private; exact control not verified. The Bahamas study is EU-financed and Expertise France-commissioned; study funding does not finance full construction.
records.cost: No independently verified current commercial fleet cost. Evaluate tropical island electricity, cooling and water separately, with a clear allocation of shared costs.
records.demand_and_timing: Could supply steady local power in suitable tropical waters. No credible delivered global 2050 share established in this review.
records.limitations: Low heat-engine efficiency, pumping energy, heat exchangers, huge deep-water pipes, biofouling and storms.
records.geopolitics: Fuel-import-dependent islands and development banks are potential early customers/funders; coastal jurisdiction and environmental review matter.
records.assessment: Interesting local multi-service opportunity. Require sustained net output after pumps and a complete project budget.

records.name: Salinity-gradient power
records.service: Extracts energy from mixing fresh and salty water, often using membranes.
records.evidence: Sweetch’s OPUS-1 tests real-water operation in the Rhône delta. A company’s estimate of 500 MW local potential is not present installed output.
records.companies: Private Sweetch; 2023 €25m Series A led by Crédit Mutuel Impact’s fund with CNR, EDF Pulse Ventures and financial investors. Exact control not verified.
records.cost: No independently verified commercial fleet cost. Lab membrane power density omits plant-level water handling and replacement costs.
records.demand_and_timing: Potential at suitable estuaries or industrial streams; no verified contribution to global demand assigned.
records.limitations: Membrane life/fouling, intake/filtration/pumping, freshwater flow, drought and ecological limits.
records.geopolitics: Utility partners and public R&D support aid pilots; water rights and cross-sector water demand constrain deployment.
records.assessment: An early candidate, not yet a proven bulk supply industry. Measure net exported electricity and replacement costs.

records.name: Lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries
records.service: Shifts electricity in time; does not create primary energy. Sodium-ion changes materials and performance tradeoffs.
records.status: Lithium-ion commercial at scale; sodium-ion earlier
records.evidence: CATL reports 661 GWh lithium-ion sales across applications in 2025 and expects wider sodium-ion adoption from 2026. Vehicle sales cannot be counted as grid installations.
records.companies: CATL is public; end-2025 filing identifies Zeng-controlled Xiamen Ruiting at 22.45% as controlling shareholder. Sales, cash flow and public capital support factories.
records.cost: IRENA 2025 global four-hour installed system cost: US$140/kWh. Delivered electricity cost also depends on charging price, cycles, efficiency and replacement.
records.demand_and_timing: Useful for daily shifting and grid response. Required GW, usable GWh and hours depend on the actual hourly demand/supply gap.
records.limitations: Duration, degradation, fire management, mineral supply and connection. Cheap cell cost does not establish cheap seasonal storage.
records.geopolitics: Manufacturing concentration and import/localization rules change price and access; chemistry changes some material exposures.
records.assessment: Strong established daily-storage option. Treat sodium-ion economics separately until delivery and lifetime evidence exist.

records.name: Iron-air multi-day batteries
records.service: Stores electricity through reversible iron chemistry, targeting long discharge at low energy-capacity cost.
records.evidence: Form targets 100-hour discharge. Great River Energy’s April 2026 plan still anticipated end-2026 commercial operation of Cambridge; no later acceptance record verified here.
records.companies: Private Form Energy: US$750m Series G announced August 2026, T. Rowe Price-led. Backlog is not an operating storage fleet.
records.cost: No independently verified complete installed fleet cost. A low materials cost or US$/kWh target excludes some project and operating questions.
records.demand_and_timing: Can address multi-day weather gaps if performance and prices hold. Quantify MW, usable MWh, recharge time and frequency, rather than a generation share.
records.limitations: Round-trip losses, footprint, manufacturing yield, lifetime and economics of infrequent use.
records.geopolitics: US industrial support and utility capacity procurement can fund early installations.
records.assessment: Potentially important for reliability. Require customer-accepted performance and a full installed price before assuming cheap multi-day coverage.

records.name: Compressed-air and flow-battery storage
records.service: Compressed air stores mechanical energy; flow batteries store energy in liquid electrolytes. They are different long-duration approaches.
records.status: Operating references; scale and economics vary
records.evidence: Hydrostor Goderich: 1.75 MW discharge, >10 MWh physical storage, 7 MWh contracted, in service 2019. DICP reports Dalian 100 MW/400 MWh vanadium-flow phase connected in 2022.
records.companies: Hydrostor: private, backed by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, CPP Investments and Canada Growth Fund; announced US$230m financing in 2026. Dalian technology involves DICP/Rongke; full ownership/funding not audited here.
records.cost: No common verified fleet price assigned. Compare complete installed power equipment plus energy capacity, efficiency, maintenance and charging cost.
records.demand_and_timing: Can shift electricity for longer durations and reduce some supply gaps. Does not add primary generation.
records.limitations: Caverns/civil works for compressed air; electrolyte, pumps, membranes and footprint for flow batteries; both depend on utilization.
records.geopolitics: Local geology, planning, domestic manufacturing and long-duration procurement determine where projects are financeable.
records.assessment: Serious alternatives to compare by discharge duration and site. Do not assume a small reference proves a much larger project’s cost.

records.name: Industrial heat storage
records.service: Uses electricity to heat a storage material and later supplies steam or hot air.
records.evidence: Rondo announced a 100 MWh heat unit in commercial operation in October 2025. Company efficiency claims describe electricity-to-heat conversion.
records.companies: Private Rondo; historical investors include Microsoft’s climate fund, Rio Tinto, Aramco Ventures, SCG, TITAN and climate funds. Industrial buyers are also strategic partners.
records.cost: No verified general delivered heat price here. Compare US$/MWh of useful heat at the required temperature, including electricity and installation.
records.demand_and_timing: Can replace industrial fuels while adding electricity demand. Stored thermal MWh must not be counted as delivered electrical MWh.
records.limitations: Charging tariff and hours, process temperature, integration, standby losses and heat demand.
records.geopolitics: Industrial energy/carbon policy and local gas/electricity price ratios change competitiveness.
records.assessment: Concrete early operating evidence. Evaluate for the specific factory heat service; it is not automatically a cheap electric grid battery.

records.name: Hydrogen and ammonia from electricity
records.service: Uses electricity to make hydrogen; may convert it to ammonia for transport or use. Consumes energy rather than creating a new source.
records.status: Commercial components; large clean-fuel projects scaling
records.evidence: NEOM project remains a commissioning/development case: sponsor now targets first product in 2027. Large project approval is not present fuel output.
records.companies: nucera ownership: thyssenkrupp 50.19%, De Nora 25.85%, PIF 6%. NGHC customer project is equal ACWA/Air Products/NEOM ownership; financed separately, with an Air Products offtake contract.
records.cost: No universal delivered hydrogen price used. NEOM financial-close value US$8.4bn differs from current ACWA project-cost field US$9.046bn; reconciliation is unresolved. These are project totals, not US$/kg.
records.demand_and_timing: Can address feedstock/fuel demand and some long storage needs. Electrolysis increases demand from Q1; do not count its output as free additional electricity.
records.limitations: Clean electricity price/utilization, conversion losses, storage/transport, water and paying customers.
records.geopolitics: Export strategy, certification, subsidies, shipping and energy-security objectives shape early markets.
records.assessment: Useful for specific fuel/chemical services. Electricity-to-hydrogen-to-electricity needs a complete cost and efficiency comparison.

records.name: Gas, coal and carbon capture
records.service: Burns fuel for controllable electricity; capture adds equipment and a CO2 transport/storage chain.
records.status: Fossil generation mature; integrated capture less widespread
records.evidence: Gas/coal plants operate at scale. A capture percentage at the stack is not a whole fuel-chain emissions reduction.
records.companies: Utilities and independent generators buy turbine/boiler and capture systems; fuel suppliers and CO2 network owners introduce separate dependencies. No selected startup ownership implies ownership of the whole chain.
records.cost: 2026 US modeled gas US$51–129/MWh. NETL H-class 2×1 comparison in 2023 dollars: US$41.9/MWh without capture, US$77.8/MWh with 95% capture including CO2 transport/storage, at 85% utilization and assumed gas price.
records.demand_and_timing: IEA 2050 unabated fossil output differs sharply: 12,213 TWh in stated policies versus 205 TWh in net zero. Captured fossil output: 53 versus 986 TWh. These are policy-dependent outcomes.
records.limitations: Fuel prices, upstream methane, remaining CO2, capture energy penalty, storage availability, water and utilization.
records.geopolitics: LNG pipelines/trade, fuel-import exposure, carbon policy and CO2 infrastructure determine local economics.
records.assessment: Essential comparison benchmark. Do not call a plant low-emissions solely because a high stack-capture rate is modeled.

records.name: Bioenergy and concentrated solar power
records.service: Bioenergy burns or processes biological feedstocks. Concentrated solar power uses mirrors and heat, often with thermal storage.
records.evidence: Both have operating plants, but neither shares the scale or site flexibility of ordinary solar PV.
records.companies: Utilities, infrastructure developers and industrial/feedstock owners finance projects; no detailed company/control audit for these two families in this pass.
records.cost: 2025 global commissioned averages: bioenergy US$86/MWh; concentrated solar US$115/MWh. These are separate project groups, not interchangeable services.
records.demand_and_timing: IEA 2050: bioenergy 1,575–2,917 TWh; concentrated solar 245–1,209 TWh. Biomass carbon benefits depend on sourcing and land-use accounting.
records.limitations: Bioenergy: sustainable feedstock and competing land/material uses. Concentrated solar: strong direct sunlight, thermal plant cost, water and maintenance.
records.geopolitics: Feedstock trade, land policy and regional industrial support affect deployment; import dependence can reappear through fuels.
records.assessment: Keep as site-specific benchmarks. Neither an assumed carbon-neutral biomass supply nor a globally portable solar-thermal price is justified.

records.name: Solar power in space
records.group: Generation in orbit / transmission to Earth
records.service: Solar panels supplying a spacecraft and orbital systems beaming power to Earth provide different services.
records.status: Orbital solar established; large Earth-delivery system unproven
records.evidence: NASA’s 2024 study models two conceptual space-to-Earth designs, not operating utilities. It does not evaluate every later proposal.
records.companies: Space agencies, spacecraft suppliers and private developers have different procurement models. A current space-company ownership/funding audit is reserved for the separate space comparison.
records.cost: NASA concept estimates: US$0.61 and US$1.59/kWh in FY2022 dollars. These are design-specific modeled lifecycle costs, not present commercial bids or a universal limit.
records.demand_and_timing: No verified meaningful Earth-grid supply contribution assigned. Lunar/Mars local power must be modeled against local loads, storage, delivered mass and replacement constraints.
records.limitations: Launch/manufacture, deployment, beam losses/receivers, maintenance and orbital environment; in-space loads also need thermal rejection.
records.geopolitics: Launch access, export controls, spectrum and international coordination affect deployment.
records.assessment: Separate in-space use from Earth delivery. The Earth technology assessment cannot settle Moon/Mars choices by copying terrestrial US$/MWh.
